text: The highest excellence is like (that of) water. The excellence of water appears in its benefiting all things, and in its occupying, without striving (to the contrary), the low place which all men dislike. Hence (its way) is near to (that of) the Tao.
note: humility; serving without striving for status

tags.when_helps: Someone drawn to serve quietly without striving, finding a model in water.

display_text: The highest excellence is like (that of) water. The excellence of water appears in its benefiting all things, and in its occupying, without striving (to the contrary), the low place which all men dislike. Hence (its way) is near to (that of) the Tao.
plain: The highest goodness is like water: it benefits everything and, without struggling, settles in the low places everyone avoids. That is why it comes close to the Tao.
core_idea: Highest goodness is humble and helpful like water

text: It is better to leave a vessel unfilled, than to attempt to carry it when it is full. If you keep feeling a point that has been sharpened, the point cannot long preserve its sharpness. When gold and jade fill the hall, their possessor cannot keep them safe. When wealth and honours lead to arrogancy, this brings its evil on itself. When the work is done, and one's name is becoming distinguished, to withdraw into obscurity is the way of Heaven.
note: excess, ambition, success and knowing when to step back

tags.when_helps: Someone at the height of success, wondering when to stop and step back.

display_text: It is better to leave a vessel unfilled, than to attempt to carry it when it is full. If you keep feeling a point that has been sharpened, the point cannot long preserve its sharpness. When gold and jade fill the hall, their possessor cannot keep them safe. When wealth and honours lead to arrogancy, this brings its evil on itself. When the work is done, and one's name is becoming distinguished, to withdraw into obscurity is the way of Heaven.
plain: Better not to fill a vessel than carry it brimming. Sharpened points dull; hoarded treasure can't be guarded; wealth that breeds arrogance brings ruin. When the work is done and fame grows, withdrawing is Heaven's way.
core_idea: Stop before excess; withdraw when work is done

plain_judge.issue: Drops the condition of repeatedly feeling the point; says sharpened points simply dull.

note: overstimulation and craving dull and unsettle the mind

situations: a habit or addiction I can't break
tags.when_helps: Someone overstimulated by pleasures and possessions, noticing how they dull the senses and mind.

plain: Too many colours blind the eyes, too much music deafens the ears, too many flavours dull the taste; racing and hunting drive the mind wild, and chasing rare things leads people to do wrong.
core_idea: Overindulging the senses dulls and corrupts us

plain_judge.issue: Renders 'five' hues, notes, flavours as 'too many', an interpretive shift.

text: Favour and disgrace would seem equally to be feared; honour and great calamity, to be regarded as personal conditions (of the same kind). What is meant by speaking thus of favour and disgrace? Disgrace is being in a low position (after the enjoyment of favour). The getting that (favour) leads to the apprehension (of losing it), and the losing it leads to the fear of (still greater calamity):--this is what is meant by saying that favour and disgrace would seem equally to be feared.
note: anxiety about approval, status and losing it

tags.when_helps: Someone anxious about losing favour or status, seeing how gaining favour breeds fear of losing it.

display_text: Favour and disgrace would seem equally to be feared; honour and great calamity, to be regarded as personal conditions (of the same kind). What is meant by speaking thus of favour and disgrace? Disgrace is being in a low position (after the enjoyment of favour). The getting that (favour) leads to the apprehension (of losing it), and the losing it leads to the fear of (still greater calamity):--this is what is meant by saying that favour and disgrace would seem equally to be feared.
plain: Favour and disgrace are equally to be feared. Gaining favour makes you anxious about losing it, and losing it makes you dread worse misfortune; so both bring fear.
core_idea: Favour and disgrace both bring fear

plain_judge.issue: Drops honour and calamity as personal conditions, and the definition of disgrace.

text: Who can (make) the muddy water (clear)? Let it be still, and it will gradually become clear. Who can secure the condition of rest? Let movement go on, and the condition of rest will gradually arise.
note: confusion and agitation; patience lets clarity return

tags.when_helps: Someone confused and agitated, invited to wait in stillness until things become clear.

display_text: Who can (make) the muddy water (clear)? Let it be still, and it will gradually become clear. Who can secure the condition of rest? Let movement go on, and the condition of rest will gradually arise.
plain: Who can clear muddy water? Leave it still, and it slowly clears. Who can reach rest? Let movement continue, and rest gradually comes.
core_idea: Stillness clears; rest arises in its own time

text: The multitude of men look satisfied and pleased; as if enjoying a full banquet, as if mounted on a tower in spring. I alone seem listless and still, my desires having as yet given no indication of their presence. I am like an infant which has not yet smiled. I look dejected and forlorn, as if I had no home to go to. The multitude of men all have enough and to spare. I alone seem to have lost everything. My mind is that of a stupid man; I am in a state of chaos.
note: feeling alone and out of step with everyone else

tags.when_helps: Someone feeling out of step and alone while everyone else seems content, finding a companion in the sage.

display_text: The multitude of men look satisfied and pleased; as if enjoying a full banquet, as if mounted on a tower in spring. I alone seem listless and still, my desires having as yet given no indication of their presence. I am like an infant which has not yet smiled. I look dejected and forlorn, as if I had no home to go to. The multitude of men all have enough and to spare. I alone seem to have lost everything. My mind is that of a stupid man; I am in a state of chaos.
plain: Everyone else looks content, as if feasting. I alone seem flat and still, like a baby not yet smiling, forlorn and homeless. Others have plenty; I seem to have lost everything, my mind foolish and in chaos.
core_idea: The sage feels alone and lost among content crowds

plain_judge.issue: Drops the speaker's desires not yet showing themselves, a key nuance.

text: The partial becomes complete; the crooked, straight; the empty, full; the worn out, new. He whose (desires) are few gets them; he whose (desires) are many goes astray.
note: feeling incomplete or worn out; wanting less

tags.when_helps: Someone feeling broken, empty or worn out, reassured that these states can turn to wholeness and renewal.

display_text: The partial becomes complete; the crooked, straight; the empty, full; the worn out, new. He whose (desires) are few gets them; he whose (desires) are many goes astray.
plain: What is partial becomes whole, the crooked straight, the empty full, the worn-out new. Those who want little get it; those who want much lose their way.
core_idea: Want little and you will have enough

text: A violent wind does not last for a whole morning; a sudden rain does not last for the whole day. To whom is it that these (two) things are owing? To Heaven and Earth. If Heaven and Earth cannot make such (spasmodic) actings last long, how much less can man!
note: storms pass; intense emotions and turmoil do not last

tags.when_helps: Someone in a violent emotional storm, reminded that such storms do not last.

display_text: A violent wind does not last for a whole morning; a sudden rain does not last for the whole day. To whom is it that these (two) things are owing? To Heaven and Earth. If Heaven and Earth cannot make such (spasmodic) actings last long, how much less can man!
plain: A gale doesn't last the whole morning, and a downpour doesn't last all day. These come from Heaven and Earth, and if even they can't make such bursts last, how much less can a person.
core_idea: Violent bursts never last

text: He who stands on his tiptoes does not stand firm; he who stretches his legs does not walk (easily). (So), he who displays himself does not shine; he who asserts his own views is not distinguished; he who vaunts himself does not find his merit acknowledged; he who is self-conceited has no superiority allowed to him.
note: trying too hard to impress; self-promotion backfires

tags.when_helps: Someone tempted to show off or push their views, reminded that self-display backfires.

display_text: He who stands on his tiptoes does not stand firm; he who stretches his legs does not walk (easily). (So), he who displays himself does not shine; he who asserts his own views is not distinguished; he who vaunts himself does not find his merit acknowledged; he who is self-conceited has no superiority allowed to him.
plain: On tiptoe you can't stand firm; taking huge strides you can't walk well. In the same way, showing off doesn't make you shine, pushing your views doesn't earn respect, and boasting or conceit wins no recognition.
core_idea: Self-display defeats itself

note: change and reversal of fortune; effort undone

situations: loss of a dream or plan
tags.when_helps: Someone whose fortunes have reversed, recognising that things naturally turn over.

plain: Things naturally turn around: what was ahead falls behind, what was warm grows cold, strength often falls to weakness, and stored wealth crumbles, mocking our effort.
core_idea: Everything reverses in time

text: He who knows other men is discerning; he who knows himself is intelligent. He who overcomes others is strong; he who overcomes himself is mighty. He who is satisfied with his lot is rich; he who goes on acting with energy has a (firm) will.
note: self-knowledge, self-mastery and contentment

tags.when_helps: Someone reflecting on what real strength and richness are: self-knowledge, self-mastery, contentment.

display_text: He who knows other men is discerning; he who knows himself is intelligent. He who overcomes others is strong; he who overcomes himself is mighty. He who is satisfied with his lot is rich; he who goes on acting with energy has a (firm) will.
plain: Knowing others is shrewd; knowing yourself is wise. Defeating others is strength; mastering yourself is real power. Being content is wealth; persevering shows a firm will.
core_idea: Self-knowledge and self-mastery are true strength

text: The soft overcomes the hard; and the weak the strong.
note: feeling weak or powerless against force

tags.when_helps: Someone feeling weak against a stronger force, reminded that softness can overcome hardness.

display_text: The soft overcomes the hard; and the weak the strong.
plain: The soft overcomes the hard, and the weak overcomes the strong.
core_idea: Softness overcomes hardness

text:
Or fame or life,
Which do you hold more dear?
Or life or wealth,
To which would you adhere?
Keep life and lose those other things;
Keep them and lose your life:--which brings
Sorrow and pain more near?
note: weighing career, money and fame against life itself

tags.when_helps: Someone sacrificing health or life for wealth or fame, asked what they really hold dear.

display_text:
Or fame or life,
Which do you hold more dear?
Or life or wealth,
To which would you adhere?
Keep life and lose those other things;
Keep them and lose your life:--which brings
Sorrow and pain more near?
plain: Which matters more to you, fame or life? Life or wealth? If you keep your life and lose the rest, or keep the rest and lose your life, which brings sorrow nearer?
core_idea: Life matters more than fame or wealth

text: There is no guilt greater than to sanction ambition; no calamity greater than to be discontented with one's lot; no fault greater than the wish to be getting. Therefore the sufficiency of contentment is an enduring and unchanging sufficiency.
note: discontent, wanting more; contentment as enough

tags.when_helps: Someone driven by ambition or discontent, reminded that contentment is the lasting form of enough.

display_text: There is no guilt greater than to sanction ambition; no calamity greater than to be discontented with one's lot; no fault greater than the wish to be getting. Therefore the sufficiency of contentment is an enduring and unchanging sufficiency.
plain: No wrong is greater than approving ambition, no disaster greater than discontent, no fault greater than always wanting more. So the enough that comes from contentment is an enough that lasts.
core_idea: Contentment is lasting sufficiency

text: To those who are good (to me), I am good; and to those who are not good (to me), I am also good;--and thus (all) get to be good. To those who are sincere (with me), I am sincere; and to those who are not sincere (with me), I am also sincere;--and thus (all) get to be sincere.
note: responding to unkind or dishonest people with goodness

situations: conflict with a friend or colleague
tags.when_helps: Someone tempted to return unkindness for unkindness, inspired to stay good and sincere regardless.

display_text: To those who are good (to me), I am good; and to those who are not good (to me), I am also good;--and thus (all) get to be good. To those who are sincere (with me), I am sincere; and to those who are not sincere (with me), I am also sincere;--and thus (all) get to be sincere.
plain: I am good to those who are good to me and also to those who are not, and so everyone becomes good. I am sincere with the sincere and also with the insincere, and so everyone becomes sincere.
core_idea: Return goodness to all, and goodness spreads

text: Misery!--happiness is to be found by its side! Happiness!--misery lurks beneath it! Who knows what either will come to in the end?
note: good and bad fortune intertwined; uncertainty about outcomes

tags.when_helps: Someone in good or bad fortune, reminded that neither is fixed and no one knows what follows.

display_text: Misery!--happiness is to be found by its side! Happiness!--misery lurks beneath it! Who knows what either will come to in the end?
plain: Happiness sits right beside misery, and misery hides beneath happiness. Who knows how either will turn out in the end?
core_idea: Fortune and misfortune are intertwined

text: He who lightly promises is sure to keep but little faith; he who is continually thinking things easy is sure to find them difficult. Therefore the sage sees difficulty even in what seems easy, and so never has any difficulties.
note: overcommitting; underestimating tasks

tags.when_helps: Someone tempted to underestimate a task or promise too lightly.

display_text: He who lightly promises is sure to keep but little faith; he who is continually thinking things easy is sure to find them difficult. Therefore the sage sees difficulty even in what seems easy, and so never has any difficulties.
plain: People who promise easily rarely keep their word, and those who assume everything is easy find it hard. So the sage treats even easy-looking things as difficult, and so meets no difficulties.
core_idea: Treat easy things seriously to avoid trouble

text: The tree which fills the arms grew from the tiniest sprout; the tower of nine storeys rose from a (small) heap of earth; the journey of a thousand li commenced with a single step.
note: overwhelmed by a big goal; starting small

tags.when_helps: Someone daunted by a big undertaking, reminded that everything great starts small.

display_text: The tree which fills the arms grew from the tiniest sprout; the tower of nine storeys rose from a (small) heap of earth; the journey of a thousand li commenced with a single step.
plain: A tree too wide to hug grew from a tiny sprout; a nine-storey tower began as a small pile of earth; a thousand-mile journey starts with one step.
core_idea: Great things begin small

text: To know and yet (think) we do not know is the highest (attainment); not to know (and yet think) we do know is a disease.
note: humility about what we know; overconfidence

tags.when_helps: Someone wrestling with what they know or don't, invited to value humility about knowledge.

display_text: To know and yet (think) we do not know is the highest (attainment); not to know (and yet think) we do know is a disease.
plain: Knowing, yet thinking you don't know, is the highest state; not knowing, yet thinking you do, is a sickness.
core_idea: Thinking you know when you don't is sickness

text: Man at his birth is supple and weak; at his death, firm and strong. (So it is with) all things. Trees and plants, in their early growth, are soft and brittle; at their death, dry and withered. Thus it is that firmness and strength are the concomitants of death; softness and weakness, the concomitants of life.
note: rigidity versus flexibility; staying open

situations: conflict with a friend or colleague
tags.when_helps: Someone being rigid or hard-headed, reminded that flexibility belongs to life.

display_text: Man at his birth is supple and weak; at his death, firm and strong. (So it is with) all things. Trees and plants, in their early growth, are soft and brittle; at their death, dry and withered. Thus it is that firmness and strength are the concomitants of death; softness and weakness, the concomitants of life.
plain: At birth people are soft and weak; at death, stiff and hard. Plants are tender when young and dry and brittle when dead. So hardness and rigidity go with death, softness and weakness with life.
core_idea: Softness belongs to life, rigidity to death

text: When a reconciliation is effected (between two parties) after a great animosity, there is sure to be a grudge remaining (in the mind of the one who was wrong). And how can this be beneficial (to the other)?
note: lingering resentment after making up

situations: conflict with a friend or colleague
tags.when_helps: Someone who reconciled after a bitter quarrel yet still feels a grudge lingering.

display_text: When a reconciliation is effected (between two parties) after a great animosity, there is sure to be a grudge remaining (in the mind of the one who was wrong). And how can this be beneficial (to the other)?
plain: After a bitter quarrel is patched up, some resentment always remains, and how can that be good?
core_idea: Reconciliation after enmity leaves resentment

plain_judge.issue: Drops that the grudge stays with the one who was wrong.

text: Sincere words are not fine; fine words are not sincere. Those who are skilled (in the Tao) do not dispute (about it); the disputatious are not skilled in it. Those who know (the Tao) are not extensively learned; the extensively learned do not know it.
note: flattery versus honesty; arguing to win

situations: conflict with a friend or colleague
tags.when_helps: Someone caught in arguments or dazzled by eloquence, reminded that truth is plain.

display_text: Sincere words are not fine; fine words are not sincere. Those who are skilled (in the Tao) do not dispute (about it); the disputatious are not skilled in it. Those who know (the Tao) are not extensively learned; the extensively learned do not know it.
plain: True words aren't fancy, and fancy words aren't true. Those skilled in the Tao don't argue; those who argue aren't skilled. Those who know it aren't widely learned; the widely learned don't know it.
core_idea: Truth is plain; wisdom needs no argument

text: The sage does not accumulate (for himself). The more that he expends for others, the more does he possess of his own; the more that he gives to others, the more does he have himself.
note: generosity; giving enriches the giver

tags.when_helps: Someone holding tightly to what they have, invited to see that giving makes one richer.

display_text: The sage does not accumulate (for himself). The more that he expends for others, the more does he possess of his own; the more that he gives to others, the more does he have himself.
plain: The sage doesn't hoard. The more he spends on others, the more he has; the more he gives, the richer he becomes.
core_idea: Giving to others enriches the giver
